failures.expected: pUC19 pasted as a GenBank ORIGIN block denotes the same 2686 bp molecule: template_length 2686, EcoRI site [395], cut [396], fragment lengths [396, 2290]. Biopython's FormattedSeq strips string.whitespace + string.digits before searching, which is exactly the coordinate space /primers/digest's own cut positions live in.
failures.actual: template_length 2846, EcoRI site [413], cut [396], fragment lengths [396, 2450]. The router strips only ' ' and '\n' (backend/routers/primers.py:597 and :667), so the 160 digit characters stay in the template: the site finder indexes the digit-bearing string while the digest's cut positions come back from Bio.Restriction in the digit-free one.
failures.why: The cut at 396 is right for the clean sequence and wrong for the string the app then slices: fragment 1 is reported as 'GTAAAACGACGGCCAGTGAATTCGAGCTC…', i.e. the EcoRI site sits 17 bases inside a fragment that is supposed to start at the cut. template_length (2846) is not the length of any molecule, and the two fragments sum to 2846 rather than 2686. Nothing about the expectation depends on a position convention: the app is internally inconsistent for one request body.

failures.expected: same as above for pUC19 wrapped at 60 columns with CRLF line endings: template_length 2686, site [395], cut [396], fragments [396, 2290]
failures.actual: template_length 2730, site [401], cut [396], fragments [396, 2334] — the 44 CR characters are not stripped
failures.why: Same root cause, and the likeliest one to reach a user: a sequence copied out of a Windows text file or a CRLF FASTA into the GUI's template box. gui/panels/primers_panel.py:368 and :404 apply the same two-character normalisation before calling the routers, so the GUI inherits it. Where a CR falls inside a recognition site the site is not shifted but lost outright (a 13 bp probe with 'AAG\r\nAATTCAA' reports zero EcoRI sites while /digest reports one cut).

failures.expected: every character of every reported fragment sequence is in ACGT
failures.actual: stray characters ['1','2','4','6','8',…]; the first fragment's sequence begins '1TCGCGCGTTTCGGTGATGACGG' and contains the embedded ORIGIN line numbers
failures.why: A DigestFragment.sequence is consumed downstream as DNA — the Assembly tab ligates the most recent digest's fragments (gui/panels/primers_panel.py:379 stores _last_digest), and backend/workflow/engine.py:112 feeds digest output into workflow steps. Coordinates aside, these strings are not sequences.

failures.expected: every character of every reported fragment sequence is in ACGT
failures.actual: stray character ['\r'] — 44 carriage returns distributed through the fragment sequences
failures.why: Same defect as above; recorded separately because the CRLF input is the more plausible paste and its fragment lengths (396 + 2334) are inflated by exactly the 44 CRs.

failures.expected: for one request body, cut == site start + fst5 (EcoRI fst5 = 1), so site [413] would have to come with cut [414], and site [395] with cut [396]
failures.actual: /primers/restriction_sites says the site starts at 413; /primers/digest says the cut is at 396 — a 17-base contradiction between the two endpoints
failures.why: This is the convention-free statement of the same bug: whichever coordinate space is 'correct', the two endpoints cannot both be describing it. The GUI shows the two side by side — the Restriction tab's Positions column from one endpoint, the Digest tab's start/end columns from the other, on the same pasted template.

failures.expected: site [395] with cut [396] (equivalently: site s implies cut s+1)
failures.why: Same contradiction with CRLF input. The clean-sequence parametrisation of this test passes, and test_re_12_coherence_holds_across_the_panel confirms the rule holds for all 24 panel enzymes on well-formed input, so the failure isolates to normalisation.

failures.expected: for template '>pUC19\n' + pUC19 — which Biopython refuses with TypeError('Invalid character found in …') — both endpoints answer 4xx, the way /primers/digest already answers 400 for an unknown enzyme name
failures.actual: POST /primers/digest -> HTTP 500 Internal Server Error (the TypeError from FormattedSeq propagates unhandled out of the router); POST /primers/restriction_sites -> HTTP 200 with EcoRI positions [401], computed by regex over the raw string including the header
failures.why: Two defects in one input: an unhandled exception where the router already has an HTTPException(400) path for bad input three lines earlier (backend/routers/primers.py:670-672), and a 200 that reports positions in a string the pinned authority says is not a sequence. A user pasting FASTA with its header left in gets 'Error: Invalid character found in >PUC19TCGCGC…' from the Digest tab and plausible-looking wrong numbers from the Restriction tab.

failures.expected: digest(['AvaI','KpnI']) == digest(['KpnI','AvaI']). Both enzymes cut pUC19 at the same 0-based top-strand position 412 (AvaI site CYCGRG at 411, fst5 1, ovhg -4; KpnI site GGTACC at 407, fst5 5, ovhg +4), so the reported end chemistry must not depend on list order.
failures.actual: ['AvaI','KpnI'] reports the 412 end as 3' overhang 'GTAC'; ['KpnI','AvaI'] reports the same end as 5' overhang 'CCGG'
failures.why: backend/routers/primers.py:680-685 keys overhangs by cut position in a dict, so when two enzymes share a top-strand cut the last one in req.enzymes silently wins. Both answers describe a different molecule from the real double digest (the two enzymes cut the bottom strand at different bonds), and the report is order-dependent, which no consumer can compensate for. Low severity in practice — it needs two enzymes whose cuts coincide — but it is a real non-determinism, and the pUC19 MCS is exactly where it happens.

failures.expected: BsaI (GGTCTC, not self-reverse-complementary) has one site in pUC19, on the bottom strand: its reverse complement GAGACC occurs on the top strand at 0-based 1765 and GGTCTC does not occur on the top strand at all; BsaI.search confirms one cut. Expected reported site: [1765].
failures.why: _find_sites (backend/routers/primers.py:568-584) scans the top strand only. It is sound for the shipped panel because all 24 curated recognition sequences are IUPAC palindromes (test_re_2_panel_recognition_sites_are_palindromic passes), so today this is latent rather than user-visible; the test adds BsaI to the panel dicts to exercise the code path. Flagging it because (a) the panel is a one-line list that has already been edited (#34), (b) the sibling Golden Gate code already relies on Type IIS enzymes — BsaI, BsmBI, Esp3I, BbsI at backend/routers/cloning.py:342-344 — all non-palindromic, so the two halves of the app disagree about what a site search means, and (c) the failure mode is a silent miss, not an error.

failures.expected: the two endpoints agree on how many times BsaI cuts: /primers/digest reports cut [1760] (Bio.Restriction 1-based 1761), so /primers/restriction_sites must report one site
failures.actual: digest: 1 cut at 1760 and fragments [926, 1760]; restriction_sites: 0 sites
failures.why: Convention-free form of the previous finding: /digest delegates to Bio.Restriction and therefore searches both strands, while /restriction_sites uses its own top-strand regex. Same enzyme, same template, two different answers about whether it cuts at all.

Environment: `make venv` cannot run in this container (python3.11-venv/ensurepip is absent), so backend/.venv was created as `python3 -m venv --system-site-packages --without-pip backend/.venv` over the system interpreter, which already has Biopython 1.85, FastAPI 0.115.6 and pytest 8.3.4. The pinned corpus was copied from that interpreter's dist-packages; MANIFEST.json records the paths. Tests were run with `PYTHONPATH=. backend/.venv/bin/python -m pytest gx/ -q -p no:cacheprovider` and need no network.

Scope note: the commit was rebased onto origin/main 0ab8a85 (another party landed #78/#84 and the 0.6.0 bump mid-round); the suite was re-run after the rebase with the identical 10-failed/52-passed result, and that is the run recorded here. `make check` is unaffected — gx/ is outside backend/tests/ and gui/, and `make lint` covers backend/ gui/ oligolia.py .claude/qa/ only. `ruff check gx/*.py` is clean; ruff flags one unused import inside the pinned corpus copy of Biopython's Restriction.py, which must stay byte-identical and is not linted by any project target.

What passed, and so is now evidence rather than assumption: site starts and cut positions for all 24 panel enzymes on linear and circular pUC19; the cut convention (0-based, top strand, Bio position - 1, site start + fst5) for EcoRI/NdeI/SmaI/KpnI/PvuII; origin-spanning sites found exactly once across nine rotations; n cuts -> n+1 linear fragments and n circular fragments against Biopython's own catalyse(), including the 15-cut whole-panel digest; the ten no-site enzymes; overlapping same-enzyme and cross-enzyme sites; IUPAC expansion for AvaI (CYCGRG) and AvaII (GGWCC); reverse-strand mirror positions. Beyond the sealed tests I also fuzzed the app against index-derived and Bio.Restriction oracles (all 2686 rotations of pUC19 for six enzymes; 10000 random templates of length 4-30 across ten enzymes, linear and circular, checking site starts, cut positions, fragment sequences, length sums and circular overhang bases): zero mismatches. The core geometry is solid; every defect this round is at the input boundary or in cross-endpoint coherence.

For the orchestrator: gx/TRACE.md maps each gx-re-<n> id in tests.json to its pytest node id (test function names carry the RE-<n> requirement id, so a failing node id names its requirement directly). RE-3's two tests are the only ones that touch module state: the `panel_with` fixture monkeypatches backend.routers.primers.RESTRICTION_ENZYMES/_ENZYMES to add BsaI and restores them, because the shipped panel contains no non-palindromic enzyme to exercise the code path with. If a verifier judges that out of bounds for a round-1 seal, RE-3's finding downgrades from 'defect' to 'latent, guard the assumption' — RE-2 records the assumption it depends on. Nothing under backend/ or gui/ was modified.
